newsitem.title: USA: TI earnings soar on strong semiconductor sales.
newsitem.headline: TI earnings soar on strong semiconductor sales.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc. ran up powerful second-quarter earnings, it said Tuesday, boosted by strong revenues for its newest computer chips and higher operating margins.
The Dallas-based semiconductor giant's second-quarter net income soared to $249 million, or $1.26 a share, from $76 million, or 39 cents a share, in the same period last year.

Its profits from continuing operations and excluding special items jumped to $213 million, or $1.07 a share, from $41 million, or 21 cents a share. Revenues rose 7 percent from $2.4 billion to $2.56 billion.
Industry analysts had forecast earnings per share of about 87 cents and the company's stock soared in active trading after it reported its results.
Texas Instruments' stock added $9.625, or 10 percent, to $107.125 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the most actively traded issues.
Company executives said key semiconductor revenues rose 17 percent from the same quarter last year and were 10 percent higher than in the first quarter of 1997.
Operating profits from semiconductors rose fourfold from the second quarter of 1996 and 45 percent from the first quarter.

"This was a very good quarter," President and Chief Executive Thomas Engibous said in a statement. "We realise the opportunity for TI is significant, especially as digital signal processing becomes the core element in a growing number of electronic products."
Digital signal processors, or DSPs, which are primarily used in wireless communications and the audio and video functions of electronic equipment, are at the core of TI's strategy.

With the recent sale of its defence, notebook and software divisions, semiconductors now account for 80 percent of the company's revenues, and fast-growing DSPs make up more than 40 percent of semiconductor sales.
"We are moving quickly and aggressively to extend our leadership in this rapidly growing market," Engibous said.
The company said its newest DSP, the so-called 'C6x, had been chosen by most major Internet-access equipment providers for their advanced designs.
Last year's second-quarter results were battered by a sharp decline in prices for dynamic random access memory chips and the chip market so far has struggled to rebound.

TI said Tuesday that its DRAM losses had continued to narrow in the latest quarter but that pricing pressures increased toward the end of the period and the market would remain volatile in the near-term.

Despite the problems with DRAMs, semiconductor orders were 72 percent higher than in the year-ago period. The company said semiconductor orders, excluding memory chips, were also up over the first quarter but gave no further details.

"TI's outlook for longer-term semiconductor market growth remains positive, and plans for 1997 continue to be based on a moderate market recovery," the company said, adding that it might spend a little more than the $1.1 billion it had originally forecast for capital spending in 1997.

TI's operating profit margin, excluding special charges, rose to 13 percent from 2 percent in the second quarter last year, with margins in the semiconductor division up 10 percentage points from the year-ago period and 4 percentage points from the first quarter.

Revenues and profit from operations in TI's materials and controls business rose 5 percent and 46 percent, respectively, in part because of increased demand for radio frequency identification systems. Calculator revenues were up 19 percent from the same period last year.

Second quarter results included two special pretax items: an operating charge of $44 million for the termination of joint-venture agreements in Thailand, and a $66 million gain from the sale of three TI businesses. They included its software division, bought by Sterling Software for $165 million.
